title: Gaza-Based Drama The Voice of Hind Rajab Witnesses 23-Minute Ovation At Venice Fest | Hollywood News - News18
text: A powerful reminder of the human toll of war took centre stage at the Venice Film Festival as The Voice of Hind Rajab premiered to overwhelming applause. The Gaza-based docu-drama, directed by Franco-Tunisian filmmaker Kaouther Ben Hania, received a 23-minute standing ovation. Moreover, the audience members were moved to tears, chanting “Free, Free Palestine" and waving flags in solidarity. The film revisits the tragic story of Hind Rajab, a six-year-old girl killed in Gaza on January 29, 2024, while trapped in a car under Israeli fire. Using authentic audio from the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, Ben Hania captures Hind’s desperate final moments. In one harrowing recording, the child pleads, “Please come to me, please come. I’m scared." Despite repeated calls for help, rescue was delayed. Hind was later found dead inside the vehicle alongside her family members. Reports revealed that the Israeli military blocked an ambulance from reaching her for nearly three hours. Two paramedics who attempted the mission were also killed, and their bodies discovered with the car. Ahead of the screening, Ben Hania talked about her motivation for telling the story. She criticised the way civilian deaths are often reduced to impersonal statistics. “And I think this is so dehumanising, and that’s why cinema, art and every kind of expression is very important to give those people a voice and face," she said at the event. Independent investigations have since raised serious questions about the incident. Research by Al Jazeera, Forensic Architecture and Earshot indicated that an Israeli tank was stationed between 13 and 23 metres from the car when the attack took place. A United Nations inquiry in July 2024 echoed these findings, concluding that the shots came from “very close range using a type of weapon that can only be attributed to the Israeli forces." The Israeli military has rejected this assessment, maintaining that its troops were not in firing range at the time. In response to recent questions, it confirmed the case remains under review but declined to comment further. For Hind’s mother, Wissam Hamada, the film is more than a tribute, it is a plea for justice and change. “The whole world has left us to die, to go hungry, to live in fear and to be forcibly displaced without doing anything," she told AFP.
